newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Nestle shares jump as 1996 profit soars.
newsitem.headline: Nestle shares jump as 1996 profit soars.

text.p: Shares of Nestle SA jumped on Wednesday after the world's biggest food company reported 1996 group net profit rose 16.6 percent to 3.40 billion Swiss francs and proposed raising its dividend to 30 francs per share.

The result was well above analysts' consensus forecast that consolidated profit would rise 10.5 percent to 3.23 billion and the Vevey-based food and beverages giant would boost its dividend to 28 francs from 26.5 francs.
Shares were quoted 63 Swiss francs higher at 1,640 in afternoon trading, near a high of 1,644 soon after the news.
Nestle had already reported 1996 sales rose 7.1 percent as volume gains teamed up with the weaker Swiss franc to boost turnover expressed in the domestic currency.

Chief financial officer Mario Corti told Reuters Financial Television the weak currency was continuing to help lift sales this year, with turnover up by double digits in Swiss franc terms in the first two months of the year.

"Expressed in Swiss francs there is obviously very strong growth, in fact it was double-digit," Corti said. But he added it would be difficult to maintain such solid growth rates over the entire year.
Nestle said its margin on sales rose to 5.6 percent in 1996 from 5.2 percent in 1995.

The operating margin was unchanged at 9.7 percent, even though the group increased its advertising and promotional spending to support the launch of new products and increase market share, it said in a statement on 1996 results.

Restructuring costs also rose, mainly as a consequence of measures taken to improve competitiveness in western Europe. "They remain substantially below the level reached in the years before 1995," it said without giving details.

"As the result of the appreciation of foreign currencies vis a vis the Swiss franc, the net financial debt of the group increased from 6.3 billion to 6.8 billion francs, as the overwhelming part of the financial debt of the group is contracted in foreign currencies," it said.
"The ratio of net debt to shareholders' funds now stands at 29.6 percent as compared to 33.4 percent in 1995."
The 16.1 percent increase in net profit per share to 86.4 francs was slightly below the growth of net profit because of the exercise of certain warrants in the course of 1995.

"In today's meeting the board of directors decided to propose to the general meeting that the dividend be raised from 26.50 francs to 30 francs per share. The pay-out ratio will consequently amount to 34.7 percent of the profit per share."
If shareholders approve, dividends will be payable from June 11. No transfer of shares affecting voting rights will be registered between May 16 and the day of the general meeting.
The board will propose that Peter Brabeck-Letmathe -- executive vice president and set to replace chairman Helmut Maucher as chief executive in June -- be elected as a director.
